answer:
FINAL HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded)

"Among NLSY79 respondents, the Black advantage in education is inversely related to socioeconomic status: it exists only at the LOW end of the SES distribution and disappears at middle and high SES — but this holds for college-entry attainment (having completed ≥13 grades by 1979), not for BA-degree completion itself, and only when SES is defined by a composite of family income, parental education and family size; under income-only SES the low-SES 'Black advantage' inverts into a Black deficit."

SUPPORTING NUMBERS (evidence):
• BA completion (HG≥16 by 1979, age 21–22 subcohort): too sparse to resolve any Black advantage — Black 3/285 (1.05%), NonBlackNonHisp 27/1367 (1.98%), Hispanic 4/463 (0.86%); only 34 BA events total, every SES×race cell has n<5 (Black BA counts 0–1 per cell), all gaps' 95% CIs span 0 at every SES level under BOTH SES definitions. Verdict per SES level: NOT RESOLVABLE (low/mid/high) for BA.
• College-entry attainment SC13 (HG≥13), complete-case n=8,467, Black vs NonBlackNonHisp:
  - Composite SES terciles: LOW — Black 51/807=6.3% vs NBNH 42/1082=3.9%; gap +2.44pp (95% CI +0.40,+4.47), RR 1.63, Fisher p=0.018, age-adjusted AME(Black)=+2.07pp (95% CI +0.23,+3.91) → PRESENT at low SES. MID — 10.0% vs 10.3%, gap −0.31pp (CI −3.95,+3.33) → not resolvable. HIGH — 21.1% vs 23.4%, gap −2.35pp (CI −8.40,+3.70) → not resolvable. black×SES interaction LR p=0.30 (not significant as an interaction, but the low-SES contrast is).
  - Income-only SES terciles: LOW — Black 39/414=9.4% vs NBNH 326/1595=20.4%; gap −11.02pp (CI −14.46,−7.58), RR 0.46, Fisher p<0.0001 → ABSENT (Black significantly lower). MID −2.03pp and HIGH −2.43pp → not resolvable.
  - Pooled: Black 121/1298=9.3% vs NBNH 783/5340=14.7% (gap −5.3pp, RR 0.64).
• Ordinal attainment (<12/12/13–15/16+): raw shares, income-only → Black lower at every SES (e.g., low: 71.7%/<12 vs 40.5% for NBNH); composite → near-parity at low/mid (the low-SES Black edge lives in the 13–15 category: 6.3% vs 3.9% at low SES), slightly negative at high. Ordinal interaction LR p=0.26 (income) and 0.66 (composite) — no robust interaction.
• Which SES variable carries the signal: the COMPOSITE index (family income + parental education + family size). The low-SES Black advantage appears only under composite SES; under income-only SES low-SES Black students significantly LAG NBNH. Either way, the (modest, sometimes fragile) Black edge is confined to LOW SES and absent at mid/high SES.
• Wealth (1985/1996, endogenous adult-SES lens): no Black advantage at any wealth tercile — 1985 low wealth: Black 3.4% vs NBNH 7.2% (Black lower); 1996 low wealth: 3.7% vs 3.5% (parity); mid/high 1996 wealth: Black equal-to-lower.
• Missing-data sensitivity (MICE M=5 on income & parental education): income-only result robust (pooled black log-odds at low SES −0.565, 95% CI −0.932,−0.197); composite low-SES Black advantage retains a positive direction (+0.316 log-odds) but is NOT significant after imputation (−0.153,+0.786) → treat the composite low-SES Black advantage as suggestive/fragile.

CLEAR STATEMENT PER SES LEVEL: For BA completion, the Black advantage is NOT RESOLVABLE at any SES level (data too sparse). For college-entry attainment (SC13): PRESENT only at LOW composite SES; ABSENT (significantly reversed) at low income-only SES; NOT RESOLVABLE at middle and high SES under either SES definition. The only statistically robust, large-n statements are: low-SES Black students significantly LAG under income-only SES and modestly EXCEED under composite SES; no claim is made for BA completion itself, whose counts are minuscule.

WORKFLOW SUMMARY: (1) Inspected nls_raw.csv (12,686×61; race 1=Black 2002/2=Hispanic 3174/3=NonBlackNonHisp 7510; education measured only in 1979, age 14–22, HG 0–18 + 95=missing). (2) Defined outcomes: BA19 = HG≥16 (age 21–22 restricted Layer A); SC13 = HG≥13 and ordinal <12/12/13–15/16+ (full-sample, age-adjusted Layer B, complete case n=8,467). (3) SES: 1979 family-income terciles AND composite index (z(log income), z(mean parental education), z(−family size)) terciles; wealth 1985/1996 as endogenous secondary lens. (4) Quantified Black advantage as rate gap, rate ratio, Fisher exact, and age+sex-adjusted logistic AME per SES level (delta-method CIs); ordinal proportional-odds model. (5) Robustness: Black vs NonBlackNonHisp (primary) plus Black vs all-non-Black and vs Hispanic; complete-case primary + manual MICE (M=5) sensitivity; n<5 warnings for BA cells; acknowledged 1979 income topcode (75,001) and absent survey weights (unweighted); acknowledged longitudinal proxies (573 respondents ever in jail-type residence; savings/spending 1989 proxies) as secondary, unused-for-core constructs. Scripts: full_analysis.py, inspect_nls.py; outputs in analysis_outputs/ (run_log.txt, summary.json).

payload.hypothesis: Among NLSY79 respondents, the Black advantage in education is inversely related to socioeconomic status: it appears only at the LOW end of the SES distribution and not at middle or high SES, but only for college-entry attainment (HG>=13 by 1979) and only under a composite SES of family income, parental education and family size; it is not detectable for BA completion (cells n<5 everywhere) and inverts to a Black deficit under income-only SES at low SES.
payload.workflow: Inspect -> layer A (age 21-22 BA proxy, all cells n<5) -> layer B (SC13 and ordinal, full-sample age+sex-adjusted logit + proportional odds) -> gaps/RR/Fisher per SES tercile for income-only and composite SES -> delta-method AMEs -> wealth 1985/1996 endogenous lens -> MICE M=5 sensitivity -> verdicts per SES level -> hypothesis
